content: Caroline Jones reported her involvement as a co-investigator in a Wellcome Trust Collaborative Award project. This project aimed to enhance the effectiveness of malaria prevention in Africa, particularly in regions with insecticide resistance. The research focused on identifying factors that limit the efficacy of current malaria prevention tools, such as insecticide-treated nets, and exploring cost-effective complementary interventions to reduce malaria transmission to zero. However, this project did not systematically evaluate any specific tool under discussion by the Evidence Review Group (ERG). She also disclosed her role as a co-investigator in a DFID/MRC/Wellcome Trust Joint Global Health Trials-funded project. This study, a household-randomized controlled trial, investigated whether improved housing could provide additional protection against clinical malaria compared to current best practices. Neil Lobo reported his role as a co-principal investigator in a project titled Screening mosquito entry points into houses with novel long-lasting insecticidal netting to reduce indoor vector densities and mitigate pyrethroid resistance, conducted in collaboration with Durham University. He disclosed no interests related to the topics of the meetings. The methodologist and systematic review teams involved in the WHO-commissioned reviews declared no interests related to the meeting topics. Dr. Lucy Tusting declared receiving over $5,000 in remuneration for consulting services provided to WHO, which ended in October 2022. This work involved supporting the development of the WHO Urban Malaria Framework. She also received research funding exceeding $5,000 for a Medical Research Council (UK) fellowship, which continues until November 2023, focusing on the role of improved housing in malaria prevention. Additionally, she received a grant from the Novo Nordisk Foundation for risk mapping of malaria and Aedes-borne diseases in Tanzania, running until 2026. Charles Wondji declared receiving research support exceeding $5,000 from the Innovative Vector Control Consortium (IVCC). His ongoing studies evaluate the entomological impact of new indoor residual spraying (IRS) products, dual active ingredient nets, and pyrethroid-PBO nets against insecticide-resistant mosquitoes. Dr. Josh Yukich disclosed receiving salary support from his university for a project titled New Nets, which investigates the cost and cost-effectiveness of dual active ingredient nets and pyrethroid-PBO nets. He also supervises students analyzing the effectiveness of IRS and has been involved in similar analyses over the years while employed at Tulane University. Additionally, he acts as a consultant for the University of California, San Francisco, designing data collection tools for a cost-effectiveness and willingness-to-pay study involving topical repellents. Three members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) declared potential interests. After assessment, it was decided that Dr. Lucy Tusting could participate in all sessions. However, Dr. Josh Yukich was recused from decision-making processes related to dual active ingredient nets, topical repellents, and sessions formulating recommendations. Similarly, Prof. Wondji was recused from decision-making processes concerning IRS and dual active ingredient nets. Dr. Umberto D’Alessandro disclosed receiving remuneration for being a member of the external scientific advisory board for Medicines for Malaria Venture until December 2018. He also received travel support for meetings in Geneva in 2017 and 2018 and a donation of dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine treatments for a cluster-randomized trial on mass drug administration in 2018. He was also an investigator in a trial on the safety and efficacy of pyronaridine-artesunate in asymptomatic malaria-infected individuals. Jennifer Armistead reported her employment with the US President’s Malaria Initiative, which supported several projects over the past four years with funding exceeding $5,000. However, she did not receive personal funding. These projects focused on the effects of IRS on Anopheles vector behaviors and their impact on malaria transmission in northern Ghana, the efficacy of pirimiphos-methyl in experimental huts, and the impact of attractive targeted sugar baits (ATSBs) combined with IRS. Caroline Jones disclosed receiving research support exceeding $5,000 in the last four years for her role as a co-investigator in various projects, including a UNITAID-funded project on endectocide-based malaria interventions, a Wellcome Trust Collaborative Award project on malaria prevention in insecticide-resistant Africa, and a DFID/MRC/Wellcome Trust Joint Global Health Trials-funded project on improved housing for malaria prevention. She was also a co-investigator in a PATH-funded project on healthcare utilization strategies in the context of RTS,S/AS01 vaccine introduction in Kenya. Neil Lobo reported receiving research funding exceeding $5,000 and/or non-monetary support valued at over $1,000 in the last four years for projects investigating spatial repellent products for vector-borne disease control and innovative interventions for reducing outdoor malaria transmission. Melanie Renshaw disclosed receiving salary support exceeding $5,000 from the African Leaders Malaria Alliance. Five members of the ERG declared interests, but none were deemed relevant to the recommendations under review. All members were allowed to fully participate, as the ERG’s remit was limited to identifying factual errors, providing clarity, and commenting on implementation implications without altering the GDG-formulated recommendations. Their expertise was considered valuable, particularly regarding implementation considerations and factors related to gender, social determinants, equity, and human rights. No interests related to the meeting topics were disclosed by the methodologist or systematic review teams. Professor Salim Abdulla declared two chemoprevention research support grants received by his institute, with his involvement in one study as a technical advisor. These interests were assessed as related to the overall topic of malaria chemoprevention, with one interest directly related to PMC. One interest was non-personal, academic, and financially significant, while the other was personal, academic, and financially insignificant. He was allowed to join the discussions as a full GDG member. Professor Joseph Amon disclosed a research support grant received by a previous employer for activities related to MDA/chemoprevention for other diseases. This interest was non-current and non-personal. He was allowed to join the discussions as a full GDG member. The late Dr. Martin De Smet declared his employment with an organization involved in chemoprevention. This interest was non-personal and financially significant. He was allowed to join the discussions as a full GDG member. Professor Miriam Laufer declared four research grants related to malaria chemoprevention, with one directly related to IPT during pregnancy and another to IPT in schoolchildren. These interests were non-personal, academic, and financially significant. She was also the senior author of a systematic review on IPT in schoolchildren considered by the GDG. However, she did not contribute empirical data to the review. The review underwent a third-party AMSTAR assessment and was deemed of good quality. She was allowed to join all GDG discussions as a full member but was a non-voting and non-chairing participant in discussions on IPT in schoolchildren. Professor Melissa Penny declared financial research support received by her institute related to malaria chemoprevention and broader malaria topics. These interests were non-personal, academic, and financially significant. She was allowed to join the discussions as a full GDG member. Dr. Francisco Saute disclosed involvement in a relevant research project and that his employer is involved in related malaria studies. This interest was non-personal, academic, and financially significant. He was allowed to join the discussions as a full GDG member. Dr. Allan Schapira declared his role as a member of a Board of Trustees for an organization working on malaria. He did not receive remuneration for this role. This interest was financially insignificant and personal. His position on the Board of Trustees was not seen as interfering with the discussions on malaria chemoprevention. He was allowed to join the discussions as a full GDG member. Professor Robert Snow declared his employment and funding for studies on various aspects of malaria, though not specifically chemoprevention. This interest was non-personal, academic, and financially significant. He was allowed to join the discussions as a full GDG member.
